options: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of different elements that look alike
Atoms with different numbers of protons
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the SAME element (same protons) with different neutron counts.
questions.misconception: Different protons would make a different element entirely, and electrons are the domain of ions — isotopes are specifically the neutron count varying within one element.

questions.prompt: What is the same in every isotope of an element?
options: The number of electrons and neutrons
questions.explanation: Every isotope of an element has the same proton count — that is what keeps them all the same element.
questions.misconception: Neutrons and mass differ between isotopes — the proton count is the one thing that stays fixed, and it defines the element.

questions.prompt: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8. How do the two atoms differ?
options: Carbon-14 is heavier — it has more neutrons
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 has two extra neutrons, so it is heavier — but it is still carbon because the protons are the same.
questions.misconception: The protons are identical (both are carbon!), and electrons are not what varies here — the extra neutrons are the whole difference, and they add mass.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists care about isotopes like carbon-14?
options: They can date ancient objects and treat disease with them
They are cheaper than other atoms
They are the only atoms that bond
They change into different elements easily
questions.explanation: Radioactive isotopes like carbon-14 decay at known rates — used for dating, medicine, and nuclear power.
questions.misconception: Isotopes do not bond differently or transform easily — their value is that their weight differences and steady decay give scientists clocks and tools.
